title: Looking back: year one
hook: the stories, the practices, the Dhammapada, the depths
tomorrow: every teacher says the others are wrong. who do you trust?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Magha Puja: three lines, and the third the root, a mind made clear. The heart of it. Now the summit begins, and its first step is a look back.

An old notebook turns up at the back of a drawer: your own handwriting, younger, a bit unsure. The Buddha had a moment like that. After a long stretch of pushing his body to the edge, starving himself until he could barely stand, the Majjhima Nikaya says, he stopped and remembered an afternoon from boyhood. His father was busy. He was sitting in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree, and his mind went quiet, glad and settled, with no strain at all. And he asked himself: could that be the way?
screen: `AN OLD NOTEBOOK IN A DRAWER.` → `PUSHING THE BODY, NOTHING.` → `THE ROSE-APPLE TREE.` → `"COULD THAT BE THE WAY?"`

segments.voice: Yes, he saw. Then a second question: why am I afraid of that happiness? It has nothing to do with sensual pleasure. So he ate again, got his strength back, and set out on what his first sermon would call the middle way, between pushing and indulging. The path forward was hiding in a memory of the beginning. That's what the summit's first day does. Year one of this path was the first mountain: the stories, the first small practices, the Dhammapada's opening verse, in Max Müller's words, "All that we are is the result of what we have thought," and a first taste of the depths. Some of it may look simple from up here, the way a child's afternoon under a tree might have looked simple to a man who'd tried everything. The Buddha didn't climb past his beginning. He went back to it and found the path inside it. And the last week, kept for the road. Asalha: the wheel still turns. Obon: they come home. Kathina: the rains end in gifts. Rohatsu: the morning star. Losar: a fresh year. Magha Puja: the heart of it. Five years in, the first mountain is still under your feet.
screen: `WHY FEAR THAT HAPPINESS?` · `THE MIDDLE WAY.` · `THE PATH IN THE BEGINNING.` · `SIX FESTIVALS, KEPT FOR THE ROAD.` · then, large: `THE FIRST MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let one moment from your first year on this path come back: a story that stuck, a line, a morning you sat. Don't grade it as small. Rest in it the way he rested in the shade, and notice what it still holds.
Looking back: the summit's first step, the way the Buddha found his path in one remembered afternoon.
Your line: the first mountain, still under your feet. One of fourteen up the summit.

rose-apple.meaning: a fruit tree of India; jambu in Pali

Majjhima Nikaya.meaning: the middle-length discourses of the Buddha

Dhammapada.meaning: a collection of the Buddha's short verses

middle way.meaning: the path between harsh self-denial and indulgence

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 36 (Mahasaccaka Sutta: the austerities, the memory under the rose-apple tree, the turn to the middle way)

sources.quoted: All that we are is the result of what we have thought

notes: MN 36 paraphrased: after the austerities fail, the Bodhisatta recalls that while his father the Sakyan was occupied, he sat in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree and entered the first jhana; he thinks 'might that be the path to awakening?', then 'why am I afraid of that pleasure that has nothing to do with sensual pleasures?', and takes solid food to regain strength. 'Years' of austerities voiced without a number. Confirm.
Dhammapada 1 quoted from Max Müller (1881): 'All that we are is the result of what we have thought'. Please check against the 1881 text.
'The middle way, between pushing and indulging' is the lesson's gloss on the turn in MN 36 together with the first sermon's two extremes. Confirm.
